title: Migrating Source Detection and Safelisting
subtopics: Verifying that expected utilities are generated
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of migrating source detection and safelisting.
Apply one appropriate technique to a small Tailwind CSS example.
Verify the expected result and identify a common failure mode.

content.intro: In this lesson, focus on migrating source detection and safelisting and connect it to the way Tailwind CSS generates and applies utility styles.
content.why_it_matters: Migrating Source Detection and Safelisting protects existing projects from accidental regressions when framework versions and build workflows differ.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum highlights: Replacing content-path assumptions; Using @source; Handling dynamic classes; Replacing applicable safelisting strategies; Verifying that expected utilities are generated. Treat these as practical decisions rather than a list to memorize: identify the intended behavior, choose the smallest suitable utility or directive, and inspect what the browser receives.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Migrating Source Detection and Safelisting
content_blocks.code:
1. Create a migration branch and record starting package versions.
2. Follow the official Tailwind CSS upgrade guide.
3. Run the build and compare key pages and states before merging.
content_blocks.expected_output: A migration is reviewed through a successful build, visual regression checks and documented manual changes.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Start with the example, change one decision related to migrating source detection and safelisting, then compare the outcome. In a Tailwind-enabled project, confirm the generated CSS exists; class strings alone do not make styles available without a configured build.

content_blocks.title: Version and compatibility note
content_blocks.text: This course prioritizes Tailwind CSS v4. Confirm your installed version and use its matching official guide. Snippets using v3 directives or configuration are labelled as legacy and should not be mixed blindly with v4 syntax.

content.task: Create a minimal example demonstrating migrating source detection and safelisting. Include a before/after comparison and explain why the chosen utility, variant or directive is appropriate.
task_acceptance_criteria: Demonstrate at least one decision tied to migrating source detection and safelisting.
Keep the example easy to inspect, with complete utility names.
Test the outcome and document one limitation or environment assumption.
hints: Identify which listed syllabus topic is most important to migrating source detection and safelisting.
Change one utility, token, variant or configuration setting at a time.
Inspect generated CSS and computed styles before changing unrelated code.
content.expected_output: A migration is reviewed through a successful build, visual regression checks and documented manual changes.
troubleshooting: If no style appears, verify the package, CSS import and build-tool integration before changing the HTML.
If only a state or breakpoint style fails, check the full class token, source detection, condition and computed CSS.
For a framework snippet, import the stylesheet through its supported entry point and consult the current official guide.
common_mistakes: Applying migrating source detection and safelisting without checking generated styles or browser behavior.
Mixing Tailwind v3 and v4 setup examples without a migration plan.
Treating visual appearance as a substitute for semantic markup, keyboard usability or actual component behavior.
summary: Migrating Source Detection and Safelisting is one part of a predictable utility-first styling workflow.
Keep examples small, test the built interface and use version-matched documentation.
